pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📊 **Strand 4 — Handling Data**
Collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting information to make good decisions.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B8.4.1)
- B8.4.1.1 — Select, justify and use appropriate methods to collect data (quantitative and qualitative), use the data (grouped/ungrouped) to construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts and pictograms to solve and/or pose problems.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- identify numerical (discrete and continuous), categorical, ordinal, ungrouped and grouped data
- select and justify a method of collecting data and design a data collection form
- organise grouped data in frequency tables
- present data in bar charts, pie charts, waffle diagrams and stem-and-leaf plots, and interpret them

pages.title: Types of data
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Identify types of given data including numerical, categorical, ungrouped and grouped data.
Curriculum indicator B8.4.1.1.1
| **Type** | **Description** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Numerical – discrete | counted; whole-number values | number of Nissan cars sold by a company in a year; number of children in a family; number of learners in B8 |
| Numerical – continuous | measured; can take fractional values | weights of babies in a crèche (e.g. 4.5 kg); heights; time |
| Categorical (nominal) | non-numeric groups with no order | sex (male/female); marital status; movie type; favourite food |
| Ordinal | non-numeric but can be ranked in order | age group (child, teenager, adult); boxers' weight class; income group (low, middle, high); grades |
## ✏️ Example 13.1
The scores of 11 learners in a class test are 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 26, 29, 50, 45, 37 and 47. a) Are these data grouped or ungrouped? b) Group them into the classes 25–35 and 36–50.
**Solution**
a) As listed, each score is shown separately — the data are **ungrouped**.
b) 25–35: 25, 26, 29, 30, 35 → **5 learners**; 36–50: 37, 40, 45, 45, 47, 50 → **6 learners**. The data are now **grouped**.

pages.title: Choosing a method and designing a form
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Select and justify a method to collect data (quantitative and qualitative) to answer a given question.
Curriculum indicator B8.4.1.1.2
## ✏️ Example 13.2
A researcher wants to study how eating cream crackers affects people's productivity. Which data collection method (questionnaire, interview, observation, experiment, survey, database, internet) suits each question?
a) Will eating twice a person's normal number of cream crackers increase their productivity? b) Are people who eat more cream crackers more productive? c) Does a group of students study better when cream crackers are present or absent?
**Solution**
a) **Experiment** — give one group double the crackers and compare productivity with a control group.
b) **Survey/questionnaire** (with observation of output) — collect data on how many crackers people normally eat and measure their productivity, then look for a relationship.
c) **Experiment with observation** — observe study behaviour in sessions with and without crackers.
> 🧪 **Activity 13.1 — Design a data collection form**
Select a study (e.g. How much time do B8 learners spend on homework each evening?). Design a form with clear questions, tick boxes and a table for recording results. Pilot it with five classmates and improve unclear questions.

pages.title: Organising and presenting data
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Organise data (grouped/ungrouped), present it in frequency tables, line graphs, pie graphs, bar graphs, pictographs, infographics, waffle diagrams, box-and-whisker plots and stem-and-leaf plots, and analyse it.
Curriculum indicator B8.4.1.1.3
## Grouped frequency tables
## ✏️ Example 13.3
The lengths, in millimetres, of 40 leaves are given. Complete the grouped frequency table.
| 40 | 54 | 25 | 50 | 58 | 45 | 47 | 49 | 30 | 28 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 52 | 31 | 52 | 41 | 47 | 44 | 46 | 39 | 51 | 59 |
| 49 | 38 | 43 | 48 | 43 | 43 | 40 | 51 | 40 | 56 |
| 31 | 53 | 44 | 37 | 35 | 37 | 33 | 38 | 46 | 36 |
**Solution**
| **Length (mm)** | **Tally** | **Frequency** |
|---|---|---|
| 25 – 29 | ǀǀ | 2 |
| 30 – 34 | ǀǀǀǀ | 4 |
| 35 – 39 | **ǀǀǀǀ** ǀǀ | 7 |
| 40 – 44 | **ǀǀǀǀ** ǀǀǀǀ | 9 |
| 45 – 49 | **ǀǀǀǀ** ǀǀǀ | 8 |
| 50 – 54 | **ǀǀǀǀ** ǀǀ | 7 |
| 55 – 59 | ǀǀǀ | 3 |
| Total |  | 40 |
The **modal class** (the class with the highest frequency) is **40 – 44 mm**.
## Bar charts and pie charts
## ✏️ Example 13.4
A cleaner spent GH₵120 of his salary on food, GH₵80 on rent, GH₵40 on clothing, GH₵110 on transport and saved GH₵50. Draw a) a bar chart b) a pie chart.
**Solution**
Total = 120 + 80 + 40 + 110 + 50 = GH₵400.
| **Item** | **Food** | **Rent** | **Clothing** | **Transport** | **Savings** | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amount (GH₵) | 120 | 80 | 40 | 110 | 50 | 400 |
| Angle | 108° | 72° | 36° | 99° | 45° | 360° |
[[fig:m8-f48]]
Figure 13.1: The cleaner's spending as a bar chart and a pie chart

pages.title: Waffle diagrams
pages.body:
## Waffle diagrams
> 🔑 **Key idea: Waffle diagram** — A **waffle diagram** is a 10 × 10 grid of 100 cells; each cell represents **1%**. Shading p cells shows p%. Waffle diagrams make percentages easy to see and compare.
## ✏️ Example 13.5
The waffle diagrams show average mathematics test scores. a) Read the scores for B7, B8 and B9. b) In a quiz, Cordei scored 75%, Kofi 80%, Maama 35%, Kpakpo 70% and Adjoa 50%. Draw a waffle diagram for Cordei.
[[fig:m8-f49]]
Figure 13.2: Waffle diagrams of average scores
**Solution**
a) Count the shaded cells: **B7 = 64%, B8 = 72%, B9 = 58%**.
b) Shade 75 of the 100 cells (7 full columns and 5 cells of the next). Make similar diagrams for the others (80, 35, 70 and 50 cells).
## Stem-and-leaf plots
> 🔑 **Key idea: Stem-and-leaf plot** — Each value is split into a **stem** (leading digit(s)) and a **leaf** (last digit). Leaves are written in order beside their stem. The plot keeps every data value and shows the shape of the distribution. A **key** explains how to read it, e.g. 7
## ✏️ Example 13.6
The scores of 14 B8 learners in a test out of 100 are: 23, 56, 71, 89, 52, 64, 71, 80, 58, 72, 66, 95, 61, 74. Make a stem-and-leaf plot and comment on the performance.
**Solution**
| **Stem** | **Leaf** |
|---|---|
| 2 | 3 |
| 3 |  |
| 4 |  |
| 5 | 2 6 8 |
| 6 | 1 4 6 |
| 7 | 1 1 2 4 |
| 8 | 0 9 |
| 9 | 5 |
Key: 2 | 3 means 23. (Stems 3 and 4 have no leaves — leave them blank. Note the 0 for 80.)
Most learners scored between 50 and 79; the most common score is 71; one learner scored very low (23) and needs help.

pages.title: Example 13.7
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 13.7
Use the stem-and-leaf plot to answer the questions.
| **Stem** | **Leaf** |
|---|---|
| 4 | 2 5 8 |
| 5 | 0 3 3 3 7 |
| 6 | 1 4 8 |
| 7 | 0 6 |
Key: 4 | 2 means 42. a) List the scores in ascending order. b) What is the mode? c) What is the median?
**Solution**
a) 42, 45, 48, 50, 53, 53, 53, 57, 61, 64, 68, 70, 76
b) Mode = **53** (it occurs three times)
c) There are 13 scores; the 7th is **53**.

pages.title: Chapter 13 summary
pages.body:
- Numerical data are discrete (counted) or continuous (measured); categorical data are names or groups; ordinal data can be ranked.
- Grouped frequency tables use class intervals; the modal class has the highest frequency.
- Pie chart angle = [[value/total]] × 360°; waffle diagram: 1 cell = 1%.
- Stem-and-leaf plots keep all data values in order and show the shape of the data.
